chain.g: to go away, pass away, go forth, come to pass

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *gāną Proto-West Germanic *gān Proto-West Germanic *uʀgān Old English āgān Middle English agon English ago From Middle English ago, agon (“passed”), past participle of agon (“to depart, escape, pass”), from Old English āgān (“to go away, pass away, go forth, come to pass”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”), *gāną (“to go”), equivalent to a- + gone, and by surface analysis, a- + go. Cognate with German ergehen (“to come to pass, fare, go forth”). Compare also Old Saxon āgangan (“to go or pass by”), Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌲𐌰𐌲𐌲𐌰𐌽 (usgaggan, “to go forth”).

senses.d: Before now, before the present time
ex: I got married ten years ago.
When they first met in 2000, my dad told my mom how he had gotten the money. The story begins 20 years ago.

senses.d: Gone; gone by; gone away; passed; passed away.
ex: in days ago / in days agone

senses.d: Nearly gone; dead. (used in Devonshire at the turn of the 19th century)

it:fa.gl: ago (Note: like in English, fa follows the number.)

ety.text: From conjugated form of fare above; literally, “it makes”. Compare Spanish hace (although the latter precedes the number, unlike fa and English ago).

es:hace.gl: ago (Note: unlike in English, hace precedes the number.)

ety.text: From a present form of the verb hacer, see above; literally, “it makes”. Akin to Italian fa (“ago”) (although the latter follows the number like English ago).
Inherited from Old Spanish atras (“behind”) from Vulgar Latin *ad trans, from Latin trāns (“beyond”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese atras (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *ad trans, from Latin trāns (“beyond”).

14th century, via Old French and Latin from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”). Specifically of the struggle that precedes death (mortal agony) from the 1540s. By surface analysis, agon + -y. The sense of "extreme pain" from c. 1600.

ex: When the weight fell on her foot, she cried out in agony.

senses.d: The sufferings of Jesus Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane (often capitalized).
ex: And being in an agonie, he prayed more earneſtly,[…].
The world is convulsed by the agonies of great nations.
With cries and agonies of wild delight.

senses.d: The last struggle of life; death struggle.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin agōnia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía).
